# Skill^($`\infty`$): Recursive Self-Improvement for Agent Skill Optimization

Wangcheng Tao Affiliation: National University of Singapore
Email: [taowangcheng@u.nus.edu](mailto:)    Zhanglu Yan

[https://github.com/taowangcheng/Skill-Infinity](https://github.com/taowangcheng/Skill-Infinity).
Affiliation: City University of Hong Kong

###### Abstract

Recursive self-improvement (RSI), in which a system also improves the
way it improves, is a long-standing aspiration on the path to AGI.
Language agents increasingly store procedural knowledge in reusable
skills. Optimizing skills offers a direct way to achieve RSI, because
the optimization procedure itself can be encoded as a skill. Existing
skill optimizers, however, follow a hand-designed procedure. Even
methods that evolve a meta-skill confine it to a fixed pipeline and
relearn it for each task. We present Skill^($`\infty`$), which makes
skill optimization recursively self-improving: a meta agent follows a
meta-skill to optimize task skills and optimizes the meta-skill itself
using the same procedure. The optimization is agent-led. The meta agent
diagnoses execution traces, proposes candidates, requests independent
reviews, and allocates the search budget. The meta-skill defines these
steps, allowing self-improvement to rewrite them. This meta-skill is
also decoupled from task skills, refined on multiple skill optimization
tasks and then reused to optimize task skills across diverse domains. As
in deployment, skills at both levels are standard packages loaded
through native skill discovery. On 83 SkillsBench tasks,
Skill^($`\infty`$) reaches a pass rate of 60.7%, compared with 56.4% for
human-curated skills and 54.5% for SkillEvolver.

## 1 Introduction

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 1: Recursively self-improving skill optimization. Left: most
skill optimizers follow a hand-designed procedure. Methods that evolve a
meta-skill keep it inside a fixed pipeline and bound to the task skill
it evolves with. Center: the $`\infty`$ shape shows the two loops of
Skill^($`\infty`$), which meet at the meta-skill. In the left loop, the
meta-skill optimizes itself on a set of skill optimization tasks,
improving from $`m_{0}`$ to $`m^{\star}`$. In each stacked loop on the
right, the refined meta-skill is reused to optimize one task skill from
$`s_{0}`$ to $`s^{\star}`$. Right: the meta-skill at the crossing is a
standard skill package loaded through native skill discovery, like any
other skill. Each of its parts, from instructions to scripts, falls
within the scope of self-improvement.

_Recursive self-improvement_ (RSI) refers to a system that improves not
only its performance on tasks but also the procedure that produces these
improvements ([Yudkowsky, 2007](#bib.bib43); [Chen et al.,
2026](#bib.bib8)). Because each gain can then accelerate the next, RSI
has figured prominently in visions of artificial general intelligence
(AGI), from the intelligence explosion envisioned by [Good
(1966)](#bib.bib13) to Gödel machines ([Schmidhuber, 2003](#bib.bib27)).
More recently, _skills_ have emerged as a common format for capturing
the reusable procedural knowledge of language agents ([Anthropic,
2025b](#bib.bib6)). This format can also encode the procedure that
optimizes skills. Skills can thus encode both the target of improvement
and the procedure that improves it, making skill optimization a direct
and interpretable way to achieve RSI. Skills also serve as a
harness-agnostic medium for RSI, since Claude Code ([Anthropic,
2025a](#bib.bib5)), Codex ([OpenAI, 2025](#bib.bib23)), and
OpenCode ([Anomaly, 2025](#bib.bib4)) all load them through the same
open specification ([Agent Skills, 2025](#bib.bib1)). To realize this
potential, skill optimization must improve not only skills but also the
procedure that optimizes them.

Recent approaches such as SkillOpt ([Yang et al., 2026](#bib.bib40)),
CoEvoSkills ([Zhang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib47)), and
SkillEvolver ([Zhang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib46)) already optimize skills
from execution feedback. Despite differences in what they edit and how
they verify candidates, these methods share one design choice. The
optimizer follows a hand-designed procedure, and what it learns while
optimizing one skill does not transfer to the next.
MetaSkill-Evolve ([Wang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib34)) goes a step further:
each search branch carries a meta-skill that configures the five agents
of its pipeline, and the same pipeline refines this meta-skill. However,
the pipeline’s roles and wiring remain fixed, and each meta-skill is
bound to the task skill it evolves with. Some methods also optimize
skills in a setting that differs from deployment ([Yang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib40); [Zhang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib47)). They inject the
skill or prompt the agent to load it, so optimization never tests
whether the agent would load the skill on its own.

We believe that an optimizer that improves skills but not its own
procedure will eventually stagnate. RSI targets exactly this limitation.
In this work, we propose Skill^($`\infty`$), a framework for recursively
self-improving skill optimization. A meta agent follows a meta-skill to
optimize task skills and _applies the same procedure to the meta-skill
itself_. The “$`\infty`$” in Skill^($`\infty`$) stands for two loops
that meet at the meta-skill and feed into each other, as illustrated in
[Figure 1](#S1.F1 "In 1 Introduction ‣ Skill∞: Recursive Self-Improvement for Agent Skill Optimization").
Optimization in Skill^($`\infty`$) is _agent-led_: in each iteration,
the meta agent diagnoses the parent skill from execution traces,
proposes and evaluates candidates within the search budget, submits each
candidate to an independent reviewer, and selects the next parent.
Self-improvement of the meta-skill refines this procedure, which in turn
optimizes task skills more effectively. We further _decouple_ the
meta-skill from task skills. The meta-skill is refined on a set of skill
optimization tasks and then reused to optimize diverse task skills. This
decoupling amortizes the cost of self-improvement over task skill
optimization. Skills at both levels are also provided to agents through
_native skill discovery_, as in deployment. We neither inject a skill
nor prompt an agent to load one. Agents see only a skill’s name and
description and decide whether to load it. The description is therefore
also included in the scope of optimization.

We evaluate Skill^($`\infty`$) on 83 agentic tasks from SkillsBench ([Li
et al., 2026a](#bib.bib18)), spanning eight domains, and on GPU kernel
optimization from KernelBench ([Ouyang et al., 2025](#bib.bib26)). In
the main comparison, all methods share the Codex CLI ([OpenAI,
2025](#bib.bib23)) as the harness and GPT-6 Luna ([OpenAI,
2026b](#bib.bib25)) as the backbone model. On SkillsBench,
Skill^($`\infty`$) reaches a pass rate of 60.7%, compared with 56.4% for
human-curated skills and 54.5% for SkillEvolver, and on KernelBench it
reaches a mean speedup of 1.62. Without the self-improvement of the
meta-skill, the pass rate falls to 55.9%. Skill^($`\infty`$) still
outperforms human-curated skills when the backbone model or the harness
is replaced. Case studies in
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Case Studies ‣ Skill∞: Recursive Self-Improvement for Agent Skill Optimization")
show that self-improvement changes how the meta agent acts, not only the
wording of its instructions.

## 2 Related Work

#### Recursive Self-Improvement

The idea of RSI dates back to the argument for an intelligence
explosion ([Good, 1966](#bib.bib13)). Gödel machines ([Schmidhuber,
2003](#bib.bib27)) later formalized it as a program that rewrites its
own code once a rewrite is proven useful. Long a vision of AGI, RSI has
since been partly realized in agents built on language models.
STOP ([Zelikman et al., 2024](#bib.bib45)) runs a code-improving
scaffold on its own code but notes that this is not full RSI, because
the language model itself is not altered. Research on self-evolving
agents ([Gao et al., 2026](#bib.bib12)) has introduced systems that
rewrite their own logic or code ([Yin et al., 2025](#bib.bib42); [Zhang
et al., 2026c](#bib.bib48); [Wang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib33)) or search
over agent designs ([Hu et al., 2025](#bib.bib16)). More recent systems
make the meta-level modification procedure itself editable ([Zhang
et al., 2026d](#bib.bib49)) or compose data, harness, and model
updates ([Tan et al., 2026](#bib.bib29)). R² Flow ([Zhang et al.,
2026e](#bib.bib50)) trains a policy that orchestrates a skill library
and commits verified edits to it. These systems implement the optimizer
as a program or a trained policy. Skill^($`\infty`$), however, encodes
the optimizer’s procedure as a skill, which makes its recursive
self-improvement direct, interpretable, and harness-agnostic.

#### Agent Skills and Skill Optimization

Agent skills package reusable procedures as portable directories that
agents load on demand ([Anthropic, 2025b](#bib.bib6); [Agent Skills,
2025](#bib.bib1); [Xu and Yan, 2026](#bib.bib38)). This format has
precedents in skill libraries, induced workflows, and programmatic web
skills ([Wang et al., 2024](#bib.bib32); [Wang et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib36); [Wang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib35); [Zheng et al.,
2025](#bib.bib52)). A growing line of work learns skills from
experience ([Ni et al., 2026](#bib.bib22); [Xia et al.,
2026](#bib.bib37)) or optimizes them from execution feedback ([Alzubi
et al., 2026](#bib.bib3); [Yang et al., 2026](#bib.bib40); [Lin et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib21); [Tian et al., 2026](#bib.bib31); [Zhang et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib47); [Feng et al., 2026](#bib.bib10)).
SkillEvolver ([Zhang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib46)) writes its optimization
procedure as a fixed meta-skill that audits candidate skills in separate
agents. Some methods go further and operate at the meta level, evolving
meta-skills that guide skill optimization ([Wang et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib34); [Li et al., 2026b](#bib.bib19)), multi-agent system
design ([Lin et al., 2026a](#bib.bib20)), or context engineering ([Ye
et al., 2026](#bib.bib41)). These methods still evolve the meta-skill
with a hand-designed procedure. MetaSkill-Evolve ([Wang et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib34)), for instance, fixes the roles and wiring of its
five-agent pipeline and binds each meta-skill to the task skill it
evolves with. Skill^($`\infty`$) instead writes an agent-led
optimization procedure into the meta-skill and refines it through
self-improvement on several skill optimization tasks. Decoupled from
task skills, the same meta-skill then optimizes diverse task skills.

#### Prompt and Context Optimization

Skill optimization builds on prompt optimization. Early methods select
instructions that a language model proposes ([Zhou et al.,
2023](#bib.bib53); [Yang et al., 2024](#bib.bib39)) or evolve
populations of prompts ([Guo et al., 2024](#bib.bib14); [Fernando
et al., 2024](#bib.bib11)). Subsequent methods optimize compound systems
of model calls ([Yuksekgonul et al., 2025](#bib.bib44); [Khattab et al.,
2024](#bib.bib17); [Agrawal et al., 2026](#bib.bib2)), accumulate
strategies in evolving contexts ([Suzgun et al., 2026](#bib.bib28);
[Zhang et al., 2026f](#bib.bib51)), or meta-learn system prompts that
transfer across tasks ([Choi et al., 2025](#bib.bib9); [Tao et al.,
2026](#bib.bib30)). These methods optimize text that the surrounding
system inserts into the model’s context. By contrast, Skill^($`\infty`$)
optimizes skills, which bundle executable scripts and reference files,
are loaded only when the agent judges them useful, and can even package
the procedure that optimizes them.

## 3 Method

We first formalize skills, native skill discovery, and task skill
optimization by a meta-skill. We then make the meta-skill an
optimization target in its own right, so that a single agent-led
procedure optimizes task skills and the meta-skill alike. Finally, we
decouple the meta-skill from task skills and extend native skill
discovery to both levels.

### 3.1 Preliminaries

#### Skill Packages and Native Skill Discovery

We adopt the Agent Skills specification ([Agent Skills,
2025](#bib.bib1)), an open format through which agents across harnesses
share reusable procedural knowledge. A _skill package_ is a directory
built around the SKILL.md file. The front matter of SKILL.md declares
the skill’s name and description, while the body holds the instructions.
The package may also bundle scripts, reference files, and other
resources that the instructions invoke or cite. With these resources, a
skill can provide executable procedures and detailed conventions in
addition to textual guidance. An agent loads skills in stages, following
a design principle known as progressive disclosure ([Anthropic,
2025b](#bib.bib6)). Initially, it sees only the name and description of
each installed skill. For a skill it judges useful for the current task,
it then loads the full instructions and opens the bundled resources as
needed. A skill thus takes effect only when the agent _activates_ it by
loading its instructions. We term this mechanism _native skill
discovery_ because it is built into agent harnesses and underlies skill
use during deployment.

#### Tasks and Task Skills

A _task_ $`\tau`$ consists of an instruction, an environment, and a
verifier that returns a scalar reward for each _trial_, one execution by
a task agent. A _task agent_ is an agent harness with a backbone model
and an installed _task skill_ $`s`$. The score of $`s`$ on a set of
tasks $`T`$ is the mean reward over $`n`$ trials per task,
macro-averaged across tasks:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
S(s;T)=\frac{1}{|T|}\sum_{\tau\in T}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}r_{j}(s,\tau),
``` |  | (1) |

where $`r_{j}(s,\tau)`$ is the reward of the $`j`$-th trial on task
$`\tau`$ with skill $`s`$.

#### Task Skill Optimization by a Meta-Skill

Given a seed task skill $`s_{0}`$ and a set of tasks $`T`$, task skill
optimization seeks a skill $`s^{\star}`$ that maximizes the score on
test tasks. Our optimizer is a *meta agent* built on the same harness
and backbone model as the task agent rather than a stronger one. Its
procedure is itself a skill: the meta agent follows a *meta-skill*
$`m`$, a skill package whose instructions describe how to optimize
skills.

### 3.2 Recursively Self-Improving Skill Optimization

#### Skill Optimization Tasks

We make skill optimization recursively self-improving by optimizing the
meta-skill with the same procedure that optimizes task skills. Just as a
task skill is evaluated on tasks, a meta-skill is evaluated on *skill
optimization tasks*. A skill optimization task
$`q=(s_{0}^{q},T_{q},B_{q})`$ asks the meta agent to optimize a seed
task skill $`s_{0}^{q}`$ on tasks $`T_{q}`$ within a search budget
$`B_{q}`$. Following meta-skill $`m`$, the meta agent produces an
optimized task skill $`s^{\star}_{q}(m)`$ for $`q`$. The reward of $`m`$
on $`q`$ is the gain of the optimized task skill over the seed:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
g(m,q)=S\big(s^{\star}_{q}(m);T_{q}\big)-S\big(s_{0}^{q};T_{q}\big).
``` |  | (2) |

The *meta score* of $`m`$ on a set of skill optimization tasks $`Q`$ is
the mean gain:

|     |                                          |     |     |
|-----|------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       S(m;Q)=\frac{1}{|Q|}\sum_{q\in Q}g(m,q).
       ```                                       |     | (3) |

Skill optimization tasks and the meta score are the meta-level
counterparts of tasks and the score. The agent-led procedure of
[Section 3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Agent-Led Optimization ‣ 3 Method ‣ Skill∞: Recursive Self-Improvement for Agent Skill Optimization")
therefore applies directly to the meta-skill itself.

#### The Recursive Loop

When the meta-skill improves itself, it is both the procedure that the
meta agent follows and the target that this procedure optimizes. The
meta agent thus diagnoses and revises this procedure while following it.
The revised meta-skill is then evaluated on skill optimization tasks,
where the optimizations it guides reveal whether it surpasses the
predecessor. Such a loop makes self-improvement recursive, since
improvements to the meta-skill are self-reinforcing. Each strengthens
the procedure from which further improvements arise, yielding an
increasingly capable meta-skill.

### 3.3 Agent-Led Optimization

#### Anatomy of an Iteration

We place the meta agent at the helm of skill optimization, following a
meta-skill that is editable by self-improvement.
[Algorithm 1](#alg1 "In Anatomy of an Iteration ‣ 3.3 Agent-Led Optimization ‣ 3 Method ‣ Skill∞: Recursive Self-Improvement for Agent Skill Optimization")
outlines the procedure, and
[Figure 2](#S2.F2 "In Prompt and Context Optimization ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ Skill∞: Recursive Self-Improvement for Agent Skill Optimization")
depicts one of its iterations. The meta agent first inspects the
optimization history recorded in the archive. It then diagnoses the
parent skill from the execution traces of its rollouts. Informed by this
diagnosis, it creates one or two candidates from the parent, each
justified by a proposal. The meta agent evaluates the candidates and
submits each to an independent reviewer. Finally, it decides whether to
continue and selects either the next parent or the optimized skill.

1: target skill $`s_{0}`$ (a task skill or the meta-skill), meta-skill
$`m`$, tasks $`T`$, search budget $`B`$

2: optimized skill $`s^{\star}`$

3: $`\mathcal{A}\leftarrow\{s_{0}\}`$, $`p\leftarrow s_{0}`$
$`\triangleright`$ archive and parent

4: $`b\leftarrow B`$ $`\triangleright`$ remaining budget

5: repeat$`\triangleright`$ lines 1 to 6: defined in the meta-skill

6:   Install $`m`$ for the meta agent, or $`p`$ if the target is the
meta-skill

7:   Inspect the optimization history in $`\mathcal{A}`$

8:   Request rollouts of $`p`$ and diagnose them

9:   Create $`1\leq k\leq\min(2,b)`$ candidates from $`p`$ with
proposals, and set $`b\leftarrow b-k`$

10:   Evaluate the candidates and add them to $`\mathcal{A}`$

11:   Submit each candidate to an independent reviewer

12:   Decide whether to continue, and select $`p`$ from $`\mathcal{A}`$

13: until the meta agent decides to stop or $`b=0`$

14: return $`s^{\star}\leftarrow p`$

Algorithm 1 Agent-led optimization in Skill^($`\infty`$)

#### Search as Reasoning

Agent-led optimization entrusts the search to the meta agent’s reasoning
rather than to a hand-designed heuristic driven by scores. A score
reveals whether a candidate improved but not why, so the meta agent
interprets it in light of the diagnoses and reviews recorded in the
archive. The diagnoses can uncover a promising change that the score has
yet to reflect, such as a tied candidate that makes progress on the
failure it targets. Much as evolutionary search retains less fit
candidates to escape local optima, the meta agent can build on such
candidates instead of discarding them. It may likewise keep the parent
when a candidate’s gain cannot be attributed to its change, or backtrack
to an earlier skill when a line of revisions stalls. Beyond choosing
parents, the meta agent decides which failures to address next,
redirecting the search as new evidence emerges. In sum, search becomes
reasoning about the failure modes of each target skill rather than a
heuristic applied to all.

#### Independent Review

Only candidates that pass an independent review are eligible for
selection. The reviewer operates in an isolated context, shielded from
both the meta agent’s deliberation and its partiality toward its own
changes. The verdict rests solely on the parent and candidate packages,
the proposal, and the supporting evidence. The reviewer rejects
candidates that make no substantive change, that are never activated, or
that are unusable as written. Any gain from such candidates can arise
only by chance, and rejecting them prevents selection from mistaking
noise for progress. For a meta-skill candidate, the reviewer further
verifies that the core responsibilities of a meta-skill, including the
review itself, remain intact.

#### Adaptive Budget Allocation

The meta agent allocates the search budget itself, deciding how many
candidates to create in each iteration and when to stop. The number of
candidates per iteration sets the balance between exploration and
exploitation. Several candidates probe alternative revisions side by
side, whereas a single candidate pursues one line of revisions in depth.
Across target skills, a fixed schedule would allocate the same budget
regardless of how much headroom remains. The meta agent instead adapts
its spending to each target skill, continuing while failures persist and
stopping once the diagnosis finds little left to improve.

#### End-to-End RSI

The steps of
[Algorithm 1](#alg1 "In Anatomy of an Iteration ‣ 3.3 Agent-Led Optimization ‣ 3 Method ‣ Skill∞: Recursive Self-Improvement for Agent Skill Optimization")
are encoded in the meta-skill rather than hard-coded, so the recursive
loop of
[Section 3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Recursively Self-Improving Skill Optimization ‣ 3 Method ‣ Skill∞: Recursive Self-Improvement for Agent Skill Optimization")
can rewrite the procedure itself. Any part of the package, from the
instructions to the bundled scripts, is open to revision. Freed from any
predefined design space, the procedure can evolve beyond the foresight
of human designers and realize its full potential. Self-improvement can
remedy a weak step wherever it lies, even in the review and selection of
candidates, which a fixed pipeline would leave untouched. Optimizing
task skills reveals the shortcomings of the procedure, and each
refinement in turn yields better task skills, rendering the two levels
mutually reinforcing. To keep the mutual reinforcement genuine, scoring
lies beyond the reach of self-improvement, so gains can arise only from
better optimization, never from reward tampering.

### 3.4 Decoupling Meta-Skill from Task Skills

Skill^($`\infty`$) decouples the meta-skill from the task skills it
optimizes. The meta agent first refines a seed meta-skill $`m_{0}`$ into
$`m^{\star}`$ on a set of skill optimization tasks $`Q`$ drawn from
different domains. Each candidate meta-skill is scored by
[Equation 3](#S3.E3 "In Skill Optimization Tasks ‣ 3.2 Recursively Self-Improving Skill Optimization ‣ 3 Method ‣ Skill∞: Recursive Self-Improvement for Agent Skill Optimization")
on the inner optimizations it guides, one for each $`q\in Q`$ within the
inner budget $`B_{q}`$. The refined meta-skill $`m^{\star}`$ then guides
the optimization of each target task skill from its seed.

This decoupling separates concerns: the meta-skill captures how to
optimize skills, and each task skill how to solve its tasks. Averaging
gains over $`Q`$, the meta score favors revisions that help across
domains over those tailored to one. As a standard skill package, the
refined meta-skill serves all task skills optimized afterwards,
amortizing the cost of self-improvement across them.

### 3.5 Native Skill Discovery at Both Levels

Skills at both levels are installed in the harness’s standard skill
location and loaded through native skill discovery, as in deployment. No
skill is injected into a prompt, nor is any agent instructed to load
one. Gains measured under these conditions need no injection to
materialize in deployment. For task skills and the meta-skill alike,
activation thus hinges on the description, which joins the instructions
within the scope of optimization. Like any skill, the meta-skill is
portable across harnesses that support native skill discovery.

## 4 Experiments

We evaluate Skill^($`\infty`$) on SkillsBench ([Li et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib18)) and KernelBench ([Ouyang et al., 2025](#bib.bib26))
against baselines with and without skills. Beyond the main results, we
ablate self-improvement and test generality across harnesses and models.
We further locate where Skill^($`\infty`$) helps and measure how
performance scales with the search budget and what optimization costs.

### 4.1 Experimental Setup

#### Benchmarks

SkillsBench quantifies how much skills improve agent performance across
diverse agentic tasks by pairing each task with human-curated skills. We
optimize task skills on the dataset released with SkillEvolver ([Zhang
et al., 2026a](#bib.bib46)) and test them on its 83 SkillsBench tasks
from eight domains. KernelBench challenges an agent to replace a PyTorch
reference model with a faster implementation that computes the same
outputs. Following SkillEvolver, we optimize one task skill shared
across three level-3 problems whose reference models are a deep narrow
MLP, ShuffleNet, and a GRU.

#### Baselines

All baselines use the same harness and backbone model as
Skill^($`\infty`$). No skill and Human-curated evaluate the task agent
without a skill and with the human-curated skills of SkillsBench,
respectively. Self-generated asks the task agent to write its own skills
before using them to solve the task ([Li et al., 2026a](#bib.bib18)).
SkillCreator authors a skill with Anthropic’s skill-creator ([Anthropic,
2025c](#bib.bib7)), which CoEvoSkills ([Zhang et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib47)) adapted to run without human interaction.
SkillEvolver ([Zhang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib46)) uses its released
meta-skill to author, deploy, and revise a skill over two rounds.

#### Configurations

The main experiments use the Codex CLI ([OpenAI, 2025](#bib.bib23)) with
GPT-6 Luna ([OpenAI, 2026b](#bib.bib25)) at high reasoning effort, and
Harbor ([Harbor Framework Team, 2026](#bib.bib15)) executes the trials.
Seed task skills are instantiated from the template in
Appendix [F](#A6 "Appendix F Seed Task Skills ‣ Skill∞: Recursive Self-Improvement for Agent Skill Optimization"),
which identifies the task but carries no task-specific guidance. We
measure the search budget in candidates and cap it at four per task
skill. For self-improvement, the meta agent refines the seed meta-skill
in
Appendix [G](#A7 "Appendix G Seed Meta-Skill ‣ Skill∞: Recursive Self-Improvement for Agent Skill Optimization")
on skill optimization tasks drawn from different domains, with the
budgets given in
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Implementation Details ‣ Skill∞: Recursive Self-Improvement for Agent Skill Optimization").
We choose tasks that the seed task skill has not saturated, since a
saturated task offers no gain by which a stronger meta-skill could
distinguish itself.

#### Metrics

As in SkillEvolver, we evaluate performance on SkillsBench by avg@5, the
pass rate over five trials per task. The metric counts a trial as passed
when its reward is positive. On KernelBench, we report the
correctness-weighted speedup, which is the speedup over the PyTorch
reference for a correct implementation and zero for an incorrect one.
All reported results are averaged over 5 independent runs.

### 4.2 Main Results

#### SkillsBench

Our main comparison asks whether automatically optimized skills can
rival those curated by humans.
[Table 1](#S4.T1 "In 4 Experiments ‣ Skill∞: Recursive Self-Improvement for Agent Skill Optimization")
reports pass rates on SkillsBench, overall and per domain.
Skill^($`\infty`$) attains the highest overall pass rate, 60.7%,
surpassing both human-curated skills (56.4%) and SkillEvolver (54.5%).
By contrast, SkillCreator (48.0%) and self-generated skills (42.9%)
remain close to the agent without a skill (45.5%). Across domains,
Skill^($`\infty`$) leads in software engineering, media, and
mathematics. From a generic seed, Skill^($`\infty`$) alone among
automatic methods builds task-specific procedural knowledge that serves
the agent better than human-curated skills.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 3: Results on KernelBench. Correctness-weighted speedup over the
PyTorch reference, averaged over five trials, on three level-3 problems.
The dashed line marks the speed of the reference. Runtimes are measured
as in KernelBench on an NVIDIA A100 GPU. All methods use the Codex CLI
with GPT-6 Luna.

#### KernelBench

KernelBench probes the same procedure under an unbounded, continuous
reward.
[Figure 3](#S4.F3 "In SkillsBench ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Skill∞: Recursive Self-Improvement for Agent Skill Optimization")
shows the correctness-weighted speedups. Skill^($`\infty`$) reaches a
mean speedup of 1.62, compared with 1.18 for SkillEvolver and 1.02
without a skill. On the deep narrow MLP and ShuffleNet,
Skill^($`\infty`$) attains 1.87 and 1.97, against 1.12 and 1.39 for
SkillEvolver, respectively. Beyond whether the agent succeeds,
Skill^($`\infty`$) also improves how well it performs, nearly
quadrupling the gain of SkillEvolver over the agent without a skill.

### 4.3 Ablation of Self-Improvement

Self-improvement refines the procedure that subsequently optimizes task
skills. To quantify its contribution, we replace the refined meta-skill
with its seed and report the result as Skill^($`\infty`$) w/o
self-improvement in
[Table 1](#S4.T1 "In 4 Experiments ‣ Skill∞: Recursive Self-Improvement for Agent Skill Optimization").
Even with the seed meta-skill, Skill^($`\infty`$) reaches an overall
pass rate of 55.9%, which is higher than those of SkillEvolver and the
other automatic baselines. The refined meta-skill improves the pass rate
further to 60.7%. Self-improvement helps most in mathematics, media, and
software engineering, by 24.0, 22.2, and 11.4 points, respectively. We
attribute these gains to a stricter standard of evidence that
self-improvement wrote into the meta-skill. The refined meta-skill
confirms a fix only when the candidate’s rollout shows progress on the
targeted failure, not when the revised skill merely mentions it. The
agent-led procedure alone surpasses the automatic baselines, and by
refining it, self-improvement places Skill^($`\infty`$) above
human-curated skills.

### 4.4 Generality across Harnesses and Models

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 4: Results with another backbone model or harness. Test pass rate
(avg@5, %) on SkillsBench.
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Results with Another Model or Harness ‣ Skill∞: Recursive Self-Improvement for Agent Skill Optimization")
gives the per-domain results.

The meta-skill is agnostic to the harness and the backbone model, so
Skill^($`\infty`$) extends to other settings. We evaluate it in two
further settings that replace either the backbone model with GPT-5.6
Luna ([OpenAI, 2026a](#bib.bib24)) or the harness with
OpenCode ([Anomaly, 2025](#bib.bib4)).
[Figure 4](#S4.F4 "In 4.4 Generality across Harnesses and Models ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Skill∞: Recursive Self-Improvement for Agent Skill Optimization")
compares Skill^($`\infty`$) with human-curated skills under the same
harness and model. Skill^($`\infty`$) reaches 66.5% with GPT-5.6 Luna
and 56.9% with OpenCode, against 61.2% and 53.3% for human-curated
skills, respectively. Built on standard skill packages,
Skill^($`\infty`$) keeps its advantage over human-curated skills across
harnesses and backbone models.

|--------------------|--------|-------|-------|-------|--------|-------|--------|
|                    | \(33\) | \(8\) | \(6\) | \(2\) | \(13\) | \(2\) | \(19\) |
| No skill           | 95.2   | 37.5  | 36.7  | 60.0  | 0.0    | 0.0   | 0.0    |
| Human-curated      | 92.1   | 70.0  | 36.7  | 30.0  | 58.5   | 20.0  | 0.0    |

Table 2: Pass rate by skill-utility category. Test pass rate (avg@5, %)
on SkillsBench, with the number of tasks in parentheses.
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Skill-Utility Categories ‣ Skill∞: Recursive Self-Improvement for Agent Skill Optimization")
defines the categories.

An overall pass rate does not show which tasks benefit from
Skill^($`\infty`$). Following SkillEvolver ([Zhang et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib46)), we group tasks by skill utility as defined in
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Skill-Utility Categories ‣ Skill∞: Recursive Self-Improvement for Agent Skill Optimization").
Category A holds tasks that the agent solves without a skill. B1, B2,
and B3 hold partly solved tasks on which human-curated skills improve,
preserve, or degrade the pass rate, respectively. C1 and C2 hold tasks
that only human-curated skills solve, at pass rates of at least 40% and
below 40%, respectively. D holds tasks that neither the agent alone nor
human-curated skills solve.
[Table 2](#S4.T2 "In 4.5 Where Skill∞ Helps ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Skill∞: Recursive Self-Improvement for Agent Skill Optimization")
reports the pass rate per category. The improvements of
Skill^($`\infty`$) concentrate on tasks beyond the agent’s reach. On
tasks that neither the agent nor human-curated skills solve (D),
Skill^($`\infty`$) reaches 30.5%, against 22.1% for SkillEvolver. On
tasks that only human-curated skills solve at a pass rate of at least
40% (C1), Skill^($`\infty`$) reaches 29.2%, against 15.4% for
SkillEvolver. Skill^($`\infty`$) provides the procedural knowledge that
the agent lacks, even on tasks that human-curated skills fail to solve.

### 4.6 Budget Scaling and Amortized Cost

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 5: Pass rate under different search budgets. Test pass rate
(avg@5, %) on a subset of SkillsBench tasks. The solid line shows the
optimized task skills, and the dashed line the agent without a skill.

#### Scaling the Search Budget

We ask whether a larger budget yields further gains, given that the meta
agent allocates the budget itself. We run this analysis on a subset of
tasks, where the default budget substantially improves the seed task
skill. We then optimize their task skills with budgets of one, two, and
eight candidates under otherwise identical settings. As shown in
[Figure 5](#S4.F5 "In 4.6 Budget Scaling and Amortized Cost ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Skill∞: Recursive Self-Improvement for Agent Skill Optimization"),
the pass rate rises with each doubling of the budget, from 47.5% with
one candidate to 82.5% with eight. Even with a single candidate, the
optimized task skills far exceed the agent without a skill (12.5%). The
meta agent allocates each budget itself, so these gains require no
retuning of the procedure. Agent-led optimization scales with the search
budget.

#### Cost

We measure cost by the tokens that all agents consume during
optimization, as itemized in
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Optimization Cost ‣ Skill∞: Recursive Self-Improvement for Agent Skill Optimization").
Optimizing a task skill with the refined meta-skill requires 8.7M input
and 66k output tokens on average, close to 8.1M and 76k for
SkillEvolver. The cost of self-improvement is amortized across all task
skills optimized afterwards. Self-improvement consumes about as many
tokens as eleven task skill optimizations. Spread over the 83 task
skills, this cost adds less than 15% to each optimization, a share that
shrinks with each further reuse of the meta-skill. By reusing its
refined meta-skill, Skill^($`\infty`$) surpasses SkillEvolver at a
comparable cost.

## 5 Conclusion

Skill optimizers have so far followed hand-designed procedures. Even
methods that evolve a meta-skill fix the pipeline around it and relearn
it for each task. We presented Skill^($`\infty`$), which makes skill
optimization recursively self-improving. A meta agent follows a
meta-skill to optimize task skills, and the same agent-led procedure
optimizes the meta-skill itself. The meta-skill, decoupled from task
skills, is refined on skill optimization tasks and then reused to
optimize task skills across domains. At both levels, agents load their
skills through native skill discovery, as in deployment. On SkillsBench,
Skill^($`\infty`$) outperforms human-curated skills and SkillEvolver,
and it improves kernel speedups on KernelBench. Encoding the optimizer’s
procedure as a skill makes recursive self-improvement direct,
interpretable, and harness-agnostic. We hope that this view invites
further work on agents that improve the way they improve.

## Limitations

Skill^($`\infty`$) makes skill optimization recursively self-improving
while the backbone model stays fixed. The resulting gains are therefore
bounded by the expressiveness of skill packages.

Both levels of optimization rely on automatic verifiers, since the meta
score is computed from task rewards. Skill^($`\infty`$) therefore
applies to domains in which such rewards can be computed reliably.

Finally, agent-led optimization trades enforcement for flexibility. The
meta agent follows its procedure rather than executing it as code. The
effect of the meta-skill thus depends on how reliably the backbone model
follows long instructions. No tool enforces this adherence, which rests
instead on the meta-skill and on independent review.

## Ethical Considerations

Optimized skills bundle instructions and executable scripts that agents
follow with tool access, and an agent may activate them without user
approval. We therefore recommend reviewing what these skills do and when
they are activated before deploying them. Some SkillsBench tasks concern
cybersecurity and are used only in the form the benchmark provides.
SkillsBench is released under the Apache 2.0 license, and KernelBench
and the dataset of SkillEvolver under the MIT license. We use these
artifacts for research evaluation, consistent with their intended use.

## Appendix A Skill-Utility Categories

Following SkillEvolver, we assign tasks to skill-utility categories by
the pass rates of No skill and Human-curated in
[Table 1](#S4.T1 "In 4 Experiments ‣ Skill∞: Recursive Self-Improvement for Agent Skill Optimization").
Category A contains tasks on which No skill reaches a pass rate of at
least 80%. Categories B1, B2, and B3 contain tasks on which the pass
rate of No skill lies strictly between 0% and 80%. On these tasks,
Human-curated achieves a higher, equal, or lower pass rate,
respectively. Categories C1 and C2 contain tasks that No skill never
passes. On these tasks, Human-curated reaches at least 40% or remains
strictly between 0% and 40%, respectively. Category D contains tasks
that neither method passes.

## Appendix C Case Studies

#### The Meta-Skill Rewrites Its Selection Rule

During self-improvement, the meta agent diagnosed the seed meta-skill
from the inner optimizations it had guided. For the 3D scene task, the
inner optimization had accepted two consecutive candidates while the
verifier still reported the same link-geometry failure. It had also
selected the second candidate, which only tied the parent. The meta
agent located this weakness in the inspection and selection of evaluated
candidates rather than in diagnosis. The candidate meta-skill it wrote
requires checking the rollout of each tied or worse candidate for the
targeted failure. A tied candidate can then be selected only when that
rollout shows progress. The candidate improved the meta score from 0.55
to 0.83.

In the next iteration, the meta agent followed this candidate and
proposed a further change that tracks intermediate scores and verifier
failures across candidates. The new candidate tied its parent. Applying
the rule it had just written, the meta agent selected the tied candidate
only after checking its inner optimization on the 3D scene task. There,
the targeted failure had been addressed, and the task skill had reached
a perfect score. Self-improvement then stopped after two further
candidates and retained this candidate as the refined meta-skill. Across
the 83 task skill optimizations, the refined meta-skill selected 54% of
tied candidates, against 83% for the seed meta-skill. Self-improvement
changes the behavior of the meta agent, not merely the text of its
instructions.

#### A Task Skill Gains a Script

For a SkillsBench task that exports the parts of a Three.js scene as OBJ
files, the seed task skill fails all test trials. In the first
iteration, a rollout of the seed showed that each individual mesh passed
while a merged link file failed the verifier’s geometry check. The meta
agent attributed this failure to group ownership and coordinate
transforms. It added an exporter script, wrote the ownership and
transform rules into SKILL.md, and rewrote the description to specify
the files the skill produces. Its proposal states a falsifying outcome
in terms of the verifier’s check. The reviewer confirmed that the script
exists and matches the documented interface before accepting the
candidate. The optimized skill passes all five test trials. The boxes
below show the optimized task skill and its proposal.

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

—

name: threejs-structure-parser

description: Export named Three.js group parts and transformed OBJ mesh
and link files. Load before inspecting files or running commands.

—

\# Task Execution

Read the task instruction and inspect every provided input before
changing files. Treat the scene hierarchy and verifier as the source of
truth for what counts as a part, how nested meshes are assigned, and
which coordinate space exports must use.

For a scene module that exports ‘createScene()‘, use the bundled
exporter:

“‘bash

node
/root/.agents/skills/threejs-structure-parser/scripts/export_scene.mjs
/root/data/object.js /root/output

“‘

Replace the paths with the task’s actual input module and output
directory. The script requires ‘three‘ to be resolvable from the input
module’s location. For other module formats or output formats, follow
the same rules below in an appropriate exporter.

\## Export rules

\- A mesh belongs to its nearest named ancestor group. Do not assign
nested-group meshes to every ancestor. Export each nonempty group as a
part directory and a combined link file.

\- Apply each mesh’s full world matrix before writing either an
individual mesh OBJ or a merged link OBJ. Group-local vertices omit
parent transforms and will misplace parts in world space.

\- Write one individually named OBJ for every mesh in its assigned part
directory. Merge the transformed geometries assigned to that group for
its link OBJ; preserve all component vertices.

\- Keep names and directory structure required by the instruction.
Detect duplicate group or mesh output names instead of silently
overwriting files.

Before finishing, inspect the exporter output and validate it against
the task’s supplied tests or verifier. Check that all expected group
directories and mesh filenames exist, each OBJ contains vertices and
faces, and link geometry matches the required coordinate space and
membership. Read verifier failures and fix their underlying cause before
reporting completion.

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

{

"observation": "Training activation was confirmed and all 60 individual
part OBJs passed, but link validation failed: slewing_unit.obj had
Chamfer distance 103.0 against a 0.0002 threshold. The rollout exporter
selected only direct children and kept group-local transforms; the
supplied ground-truth generator assigns each mesh to its nearest named
ancestor group and applies mesh.matrixWorld before merging.",

"change": "Added a reusable Three.js OBJ export script and explicit
skill guidance for nearest-named-group ownership, full world-matrix
transforms on individual and merged geometry, duplicate-name checks, and
verifier-guided validation.",

"predicted_effect": "The exporter will retain the passing per-mesh
output while making link OBJ membership and coordinates match the
verifier’s expected world-space aggregates, eliminating the observed
link Chamfer failure.",

"falsifying_outcome": "Validation still reports a link OBJ Chamfer
distance at or above 0.0002, especially for a group with a translated or
nested parent, or the exporter fails to produce the expected mesh and
link filenames."

}

## Appendix F Seed Task Skills

All SkillsBench seed task skills are instantiated from a single
template. Its description identifies the task, and its body prescribes
only generic inspection, execution, and validation, with no knowledge
specific to the task. The KernelBench task skill starts from a similar
seed whose description refers to KernelBench tasks and whose body
provides generic advice on profiling, correctness checks, and timing.

## Appendix G Seed Meta-Skill

The seed meta-skill is the starting point of self-improvement, and
Skill^($`\infty`$) w/o self-improvement uses it to optimize all task
skills. Its package contains SKILL.md, three reference files, and a
Python script. SKILL.md defines the iteration of
[Algorithm 1](#alg1 "In Anatomy of an Iteration ‣ 3.3 Agent-Led Optimization ‣ 3 Method ‣ Skill∞: Recursive Self-Improvement for Agent Skill Optimization"),
the diagnostic procedure for both kinds of targets, and the scores. The
reference files define the workspace and the decision record, the
interface of the rollout and evaluation tools, and the review criteria.
The script assembles the archive from the files in the workspace and
initializes each candidate as a copy of its parent. SKILL.md and the
reference files on the workspace and the tools are reproduced verbatim
below. The front matter retains the package’s internal name. The names
Meta Agent, Task Agent, and Reviewer Subagent in the files correspond to
the meta agent, task agent, and reviewer in the paper, respectively.

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

—

name: skill-self-evolver

description: Optimize a Task Skill or this Meta Skill from rollout
reports and evaluation results through candidate generation, scoring,
review, and selection.

—

\# Optimize skills

Act as the Meta Agent in the supplied workspace.

Read this skill’s instruction references before applying them.

The \[workspace guide\](references/workspace.md) defines candidates, the
archive, the candidate budget, and decisions. The \[evoctl
interface\](references/evoctl.md) defines evaluation commands and their
results.

\## Complete one iteration

1. \*\*Inspect the archive.\*\* Inspect the archive for the optimization
target, parent, active iteration, prior outcomes, and remaining
candidate budget.

2. \*\*Diagnose the parent.\*\* Obtain its rollout with ‘evoctl
rollout‘, and also the rollouts of its children from earlier iterations
that scored no higher than it. Complete the \[diagnostic
procedure\](#analyze-the-rollout), then form falsifiable improvement
hypotheses.

3. \*\*Create candidates.\*\* Create one or two candidates in the active
iteration within the remaining candidate budget, each containing a
complete copy of the parent’s ‘skill/‘ directory. Use the rollout
diagnosis to improve the skill’s instructions and resources. Keep the
skill’s name unchanged and its resource links valid. Write
‘proposal.json‘ in each candidate directory with the supporting
observation, change, predicted effect, and falsifying outcome. A Meta
Skill candidate preserves the \[required
responsibilities\](references/reviewer-policy.md\#meta-skill-responsibilities).

4. \*\*Evaluate candidates.\*\* Evaluate ready candidates in parallel
with ‘evoctl evaluate‘. Obtain and read each completed result.

5. \*\*Review evaluated candidates.\*\* For each scored candidate, start
a fresh Reviewer Subagent without inheriting your conversation. Provide
absolute paths to the parent directory, the candidate directory, the
candidate’s ‘evaluation.json‘, the parent’s ‘rollout.md‘, and the
currently installed \[reviewer policy\](references/reviewer-policy.md).
Run ready reviews alongside independent work. Wait for each reviewer to
finish and read the candidate’s ‘review.json‘; use the same reviewer for
corrections to that review.

6. \*\*Select and return.\*\* After every submitted evaluation and the
review of every scored candidate finish, refresh the archive. Compare
the validation scores of the parent and reviewed candidates, considering
reviews, history, and remaining candidate budget, then select whichever
‘seed‘ or ‘accepted‘ node you judge best. Select a candidate that only
ties its parent when its change addresses a failure or requirement
identified in the diagnosis. Write the active iteration’s
\[decision.json\](references/workspace.md\#record-the-decision), then
return.

\## Analyze the rollout

Analyze the parent’s rollout to decide how to improve its skill. Treat
the supplied reports, complete task packages including tests and
reference solutions, and exported artifacts as read-only materials.

Start with the rollout overview and follow relevant trajectory links.
Use search and contextual reading to verify the actions and tool results
behind an outcome, including subsequent recovery. Expand your reading
when evidence is incomplete or conflicting.

\### Task Skill

1. \*\*Understand the tasks and rewards.\*\* Identify the skill’s
supplied training tasks in the report. Read their instructions and
tests/verifier source, including helpers that define the reward
conditions. Inspect inputs and reference solutions as needed to
understand the required behavior.

2. \*\*Analyze the execution.\*\* Choose trials covering the relevant
success and failure outcomes. Match the Task Agent’s actions, tool
results, recovery attempts, and final outputs to the task requirements
and verifier checks, and note avoidable detours.

3. \*\*Identify skill improvements.\*\* Compare the Task Skill’s
guidance with the Task Agent’s actual behavior. Identify missing,
unclear, misleading, or unnecessary guidance, separating skill issues
from execution, environment, and verifier issues. When the Task Agent
rewrites or gets wrong a procedure that code can perform, provide that
procedure as a script; when it needs detailed conventions or data,
provide them in a reference file linked from ‘SKILL.md‘. Propose
reusable changes supported by the recorded evidence, preserving guidance
that worked.

\### Meta Skill

1. \*\*Locate optimization strengths and weaknesses.\*\* Compare every
supplied Task Skill’s initial and final validation scores, gains, and
the Meta Skill’s training score. Select optimization trajectories that
explain improvements, regressions, or missed opportunities.

2. \*\*Analyze the optimization process.\*\* Trace how the Meta Agent
and Reviewer Subagent used evidence, modified skills, and responded to
feedback through their messages, actions, and tool results. Consult the
Task Skill versions, available Task Skill rollouts, and node and
iteration records linked from ‘rollout.md‘ as needed to verify their
diagnoses and changes.

3. \*\*Identify Meta Skill improvements.\*\* Relate the current Meta
Skill’s instructions to the observed diagnosis, candidate generation,
review, and selection. Determine which guidance would help the Meta
Agent produce better Task Skills across the supplied tasks.

\## Interpret scores

The score, ‘S(skill; evaluation_set)‘, aggregates performance on a fixed
training or validation set. A gain is the difference between two scores
under the same evaluation conditions.

For a \*\*Task Skill\*\*, the evaluation set contains tasks. The
verifier produces a reward for each trial:

“‘text

task_score(s, t) = mean of trial rewards for task t

S(s; T) = mean of task_score(s, t) over the supplied tasks t in T

“‘

A ‘timeout‘ trial is scored on the artifacts present when the Task Agent
reached its deadline; trials without a verifier reward, including
‘verifier_error‘, count as zero when averaging trial rewards.

For a \*\*Meta Skill\*\*, the evaluation set contains skill optimization
tasks. Each optimization task provides an initial Task Skill with its
training and validation sets, and fixed optimization conditions. The
Meta Agent uses the Meta Skill and its reviewer policy to optimize that
Task Skill. Measure the improvement in its validation score:

“‘text

gain(m, q) = S(final Task Skill produced by m; V_q) - S(initial Task
Skill; V_q)

S(m; Q) = mean of gain(m, q) over the supplied skill optimization tasks
q in Q

“‘

Here ‘V_q‘ is the validation set for the Task Skill in optimization task
‘q‘.

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

\# Optimization workspace

‘WORKSPACE‘ is the path supplied in the optimization request.
‘context.json‘ supplies ‘optimization_target‘ (‘task_skill‘ or
‘meta_skill‘) and this run’s candidate budget
(‘budget.max_candidates_per_run‘). Each node holds one complete skill
version.

‘META_SKILL_DIR‘ is the directory containing the installed ‘SKILL.md‘
you are running. Use that location for this skill’s scripts and
references.

“‘text

WORKSPACE/

├── context.json

├── tasks/\<task-skill-id\>/\<task-id\>/ \# Training task packages

├── seed/

│ ├── node.json

│ ├── skill/\<skill-name\>/

│ ├── evaluation.json

│ ├── rollout.md \# Created by a rollout request

│ └── rollout/

└── iterations/000/

├── candidates/i000-c1/

│ ├── node.json

│ ├── skill/\<skill-name\>/

│ ├── proposal.json

│ ├── evaluation.json

│ ├── review.json

│ ├── rollout.md \# Created by a rollout request

│ └── rollout/

└── decision.json

“‘

The archive is derived from these files. Use the currently installed
\[archive helper\](../scripts/archive.py), or read and organize the
files directly.

\## Task Skill rollout

‘rollout.md‘ summarizes training results and links to each task trial’s
trajectory and supporting materials:

“‘text

\<node\>/rollout/\<task-id\>/\<trial-index\>/

├── trajectory.md \# Task Agent and subagent executions

├── verifier/ \# Recorded verifier results and diagnostics

├── artifacts/ \# Collected task outputs

└── media/ \# Recorded images

“‘

\## Meta Skill rollout

‘rollout.md‘ summarizes training results and links to the optimization
trajectory and supporting materials for each Task Skill being optimized:

“‘text

\<node\>/rollout/\<task-skill-id\>/

├── trajectory.md \# Meta Agent and Reviewer Subagent executions

├── nodes/\<node-id\>/ \# Task Skill, node records, and available
rollout reports

├── iterations/ \# Per-iteration decisions and other recorded files

└── media/ \# Recorded images

“‘

\## Inspect the archive

“‘bash

python META_SKILL_DIR/scripts/archive.py view –workspace WORKSPACE

“‘

The archive view includes ‘context‘ from ‘context.json‘, nodes, scores,
review status, generated-candidate counts, previous decisions, the
active parent, ‘candidate_root‘, ‘decision_path‘, and
‘remaining_candidates‘. Creating a candidate consumes one candidate
unit, including an unevaluated draft; keep it in the archive.

\## Create a candidate

Choose a new directory under the active ‘candidate_root‘. Name it
‘iNNN-cK‘, where ‘NNN‘ is the iteration number and ‘K‘ is a positive
candidate number. Use the active parent as the source for this
iteration.

“‘bash

python META_SKILL_DIR/scripts/archive.py create –workspace WORKSPACE
–parent-dir PARENT_DIR –candidate-dir CANDIDATE_DIR

“‘

The helper copies ‘PARENT_DIR/skill/‘ to ‘CANDIDATE_DIR/skill/‘, writes
‘CANDIDATE_DIR/node.json‘, and returns the candidate’s paths. Edit the
copied skill and write ‘CANDIDATE_DIR/proposal.json‘. Node metadata has
this form, with ‘name‘ identifying the directory under ‘skill/‘:

“‘json

{

"node_id": "i000-c1",

"parent_id": "seed",

"iteration_id": "i000",

"name": "skill-name"

}

“‘

A scored and reviewed candidate is ‘accepted‘ or ‘rejected‘ according to
its review; unresolved candidates are ‘proposed‘. The archive exposes
each scored node’s ‘validation_score‘ from its ‘evaluation.json‘.

\## Record the decision

Write one ‘decision.json‘ in the active iteration:

“‘json

{

"action": "continue",

"selected_node_id": "i000-c1",

"reason": "Evidence-grounded selection rationale and next optimization
direction."

}

“‘

Write exactly these three keys. Use ‘continue‘ when the run continues:
‘selected_node_id‘ becomes the next iteration’s parent. Use ‘stop‘ when
the run ends, because the candidate budget is exhausted or you choose to
finish: ‘selected_node_id‘ is the run’s final skill. If the candidate
budget is later raised, a new iteration continues from that node. Ground
the selection in the evidence in ‘reason‘: for ‘continue‘, add the next
optimization direction; for ‘stop‘, add why the search ends here.

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

\# evoctl evaluation tools

Successful commands return JSON. A correctable input error returns JSON
with an ‘error‘ message string and a nonzero exit status. Keep a node’s
skill unchanged once submitted to either command; further edits belong
in a new candidate.

\## Obtain a rollout

“‘bash

evoctl rollout –workspace WORKSPACE –node-dir NODE_DIR

“‘

‘NODE_DIR‘ identifies the skill node to run on the supplied training
set. The response contains ‘optimization_target‘ (as defined in the
\[workspace guide\](workspace.md)), ‘node_id‘, and ‘rollout_path‘.
‘rollout_path‘ points to ‘NODE_DIR/rollout.md‘, which provides the
training score, skill activation, usage, elapsed time, and links to
trajectories and supporting materials.

Skill activation is reported as ‘Yes‘, ‘No‘, or ‘Unknown‘.

\## Evaluate a candidate

“‘bash

evoctl evaluate –workspace WORKSPACE –candidate-dir CANDIDATE_DIR

“‘

‘CANDIDATE_DIR‘ identifies a \[candidate
node\](workspace.md\#create-a-candidate).

The command evaluates the candidate on the supplied validation set and
returns JSON containing ‘node_id‘, ‘validation_score‘, and
‘skill_activated‘. The result is saved to
‘CANDIDATE_DIR/evaluation.json‘.

‘skill_activated‘ is ‘true‘ when activation is confirmed across the
evaluated executions, ‘false‘ when any execution lacks activation, and
‘null‘ when unknown.
````
